title: The Three Impostors: Eclipsing binaries, stellar variability, and artifacts
text: Because maybe takes real proof to become yes. A dip in a star's brightness can come from three different imposters. It doesn't have to be a planet. The first imposter is an eclipsing binary. That's a pair of two stars orbiting each other, and when one passes in front of the other, it creates a dip that looks just like a planet crossing a single star. The second imposter is stellar variability. That's when a star dims on its own with no planet or companion star involved, often because of star spots or flares. The third imposter isn't a real signal at all. It's an instrumental artifact
